items.title: Ronald Reagan said you can achieve anything—if you don’t care who gets the credit. Abdul El-Sayed channels that wisdom with ‘TrumpCare for all’
items.summary:
The Democratic legislative agenda is taking shape, and healthcare is at the top as rising medical expenses were a major driver of midterm election messaging about affordability.

But while Democrats will hold commanding majorities in the House and Senate when the new Congress convenes in January, President Donald Trump has reminded them that he is ready to veto legislation he doesn’t like.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed—a former Detroit health official who campaigned on Medicare for all—sees a way around that by appealing to Trump’s ego. On Nov. 12, he posted to social media a picture of a notional, gold-colored “TrumpCare” card, saying “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

The next day, El-Sayed doubled down, assuring CNN in an interview that he wasn’t joking and insisting that he doesn’t care what the public insurance program called.

“What you call it is secondary,” he added. “What it does in your life, that’s the whole point. None of us ran to name things, except for Donald Trump. Most of us ran to actually solve problems in people’s lives.”

That got Trump’s attention. And on Saturday, he reposted on his Truth Social account El-Sayed’s initial Nov. 12 appeal. El-Sayed posted “Let’s get to work, then.”

The gambit echoes a famous line from President Ronald Reagan in February 1988, when he spoke at a meeting of the White House Conference for a Drug Free America:

“On my desk in the Oval Office, I have a little sign that says: There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the…
items.t: Ronald Reagan said you can achieve anything—if you don’t care who gets the credit. Abdul El-Sayed channels that wisdom with ‘TrumpCare for all’

items.title: High-end genealogy travel is booming, offering luxe journeys to the roots of your family tree
items.summary:
My great-great-grandfather came to the Tuscan ghost island of Pianosa as a prisoner. I arrived there on a luxury vacation.

The island lives up to its name, I thought as my ferry drifted toward the sole dock on this protected isola fantasma . “Pianosa” is derived from piano , Italian for “flat,” and indeed the island crouches low to the cyan Tyrrhenian Sea , its shores fringed by parasol pines and deserted prison watchtowers. From 1856 to 1998, Pianosa was a remote penal colony—and the place where my ancestor, Salvatore Giovanni Pellegrino Irace, died.

I’d learned this family lore thanks to a partnership between Ancestry, the Blackstone-owned leader in the at-home DNA-testing space, and Kensington, a bespoke travel outfitter, which invited me to test-drive its Personal Heritage Journey. After I submitted a DNA sample, Ancestry got to work filling in my Italian family tree, with researchers combing archives in Tuscany, Molise, and Campania. “So the interesting thing about Salvatore,” genealogist Kyle Betit said on our initial call, “is that he died in prison of tuberculosis in 1894—and we don’t know why he was there.”

Who doesn’t love a good family mystery? That’s part of what draws clients to Kensington’s genealogical-based trips. The journeys average $20,000 to $25,000 per person, with the company’s travel desk handling all the details in high style.

San Gennaro, the 
main church in Praiano, on the Amalfi Coast. Adam Erace for Fortune 

For me, that meant a chartered boat from mainland Tuscany to the island of Elba; chauffeured SUVs between regions; a private guide in…

items.title: Should you stock up to prepare for outages? The U.S. intelligence chief points to COVID as proof ‘America is the most amazing and resilient place’
items.summary:
The country is on edge about the recent string of network outages, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tried to offer some reassurance but drew on an unsettling example.

Worried about an imminent catastrophe, many Americans are panic buying supplies at Costco and Walmart . In an interview on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Clayton was asked if it’s time to stock up to prepare for new, possibly extended, outages.

“America is the most amazing and resilient place, and we have been living with interruptions,” he replied. “Let’s give ourselves some credit. Let’s go back to COVID, other things. Americans fought their way through these terrible things in an incredible, resilient way.”

Wait, what?

During pandemic-era lockdowns, Americans frantically hoarded so many supplies that grocery stores had to ration necessities like toilet paper.

CNN’s Dana Bash immediately stopped him right there and asked if we could be in another COVID-like situation.

“Not at all, let me be clear. But what I’m saying is the American people are resilient,” Clayton reiterated, pointing out that officials and companies are being straightforward with what’s happening.

“I have such incredible faith in the American people. As we have this technological step change, we will handle it as a country,” he added.

But when pressed on what Americans should actually do to ensure their resilience, Clayton suggested that it’s enough to just be aware.

“How do you prepare? By knowing that systems are going to be upgraded,” he said. “They may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies…
items.t: Should you stock up to prepare for outages? The U.S. intelligence chief points to COVID as proof ‘America is the most amazing and resilient place’

items.title: A ‘mismatch in timing’: Data center power demand is growing 19% a year. The grid is growing 2%
items.summary:
The tech industry is famous for moving fast. The power grid is famous for not. That collision now sits at the center of the AI buildout, a project estimated to cost trillions: Citigroup projects Big Tech will spend more than $2.8 trillion on AI infrastructure through 2029, and a Brookings study puts U.S. investment at $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032.

The grid isn’t built for that pace. Since 2000, power to data centers has risen an average of 19% a year while U.S. grid capacity has expanded just 2% annually, according to an analysis by insurance broker Howden . Data center power use is growing 10 times faster than the system meant to supply it.

That gap has become one of the biggest bottlenecks facing the AI industry. And after this month’s midterms, in which voters rejected data center projects almost everywhere they appeared on the ballot, power is now a political problem, too.

The grid is years behind demand 

Data centers took about 5% of U.S. grid capacity in 2025. Howden estimates that to hold that share through 2030 at current growth rates, they would have to source up to 58% of their power off the grid, roughly 110 gigawatts, a level the firm itself considers unlikely.

Consumption tells the same story. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could use as much as 12% of U.S. electricity by 2028, about six times their 1.9% share in 2018, before the AI boom.

Rob Gramlich, president of consulting firm Grid Strategies, told Fortune in September that there’s a real “mismatch in timing” between how quickly data centers want power and how…
items.t: A ‘mismatch in timing’: Data center power demand is growing 19% a year. The grid is growing 2%

items.title: Being mean to ChatGPT can boost its accuracy, but your tone could have an even bigger impact on computing costs
items.summary:
Bossing around an AI underling may yield better results than being polite, but that doesn’t mean a ruder tone won’t have consequences in the long run, researchers say.

A study from Penn State found ChatGPT’s 4o model produced better results on 50 multiple-choice questions as researchers’ prompts grew ruder.

Since then, Anthropic has moved to prohibit sustained cruelty toward its AI models, and the same researchers have found that prompt tone can also affect the computing resources AI consumes by as much as 44.3%.

In the original study from 2025, more than 250 unique prompts were sorted by politeness to rudeness, with the “very rude” response yielded an accuracy of 84.8%, four percentage points higher than the “very polite” response. Essentially, the LLM responded better when researchers gave it prompts like “Hey, gofer, figure this out,” than when they said “Would you be so kind as to solve the following question?”

While ruder responses generally yielded more accurate responses, the researchers noted “uncivil discourse” could have unintended consequences.

“Using insulting or demeaning language in human-AI interaction could have negative effects on user experience, accessibility, and inclusivity, and may contribute to harmful communication norms,” the researchers wrote at the time.

Chatbots read the room 

At the time it was published, the preprint study , which has not been peer-reviewed, offered new evidence that not only sentence structure, but tone, affects an AI chatbot’s responses—and that human’s interactions with AI may be more nuanced than they appeared on…
items.t: Being mean to ChatGPT can boost its accuracy, but your tone could have an even bigger impact on computing costs

While all of the billionaires she’s interviewed on her podcast BigDeal are “wildly different,” she says in a video on her TikTok account that they’re all obsessed with what they do “almost to the point of it being uncomfortable.”

Sanchez actually got her start in journalism, winning the prestigious Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award, before transitioning into finance, working for firms such as Vanguard, Goldman Sachs , and State Street . She’s the founder of Contrarian Thinking, a media and finance education company with millions of followers and subscribers, aimed at empowering people to take control of their financial future through unconventional paths like small-business ownership. She also runs venture fund Contrarian Thinking Capital, earned her MBA from Georgetown University, and is a New York Times bestselling author. Her estimated net worth is about $17 million.

Does obsession mean in entrepreneurship? 

One of the biggest debates in the workforce and entrepreneurship is whether work-life balance can really exist and whether it’s effective.

items.title: Vertex’s executive chairman: Here’s how we got our drug-trial success rate over 70% when the industry’s is 10% to 20%
items.summary:
Corporate America is locked in an innovation arms race – a race that is turning out very few winners. Companies are spending billions on R&D, acquisitions and new technologies, operating on the seemingly intuitive premise that making more bets is the best way to approach the uncertainty of the future.

But more bets don’t necessarily produce more successes.

There’s no more extreme example of this problem than pharmaceuticals and biotech. It takes an average of 10 to 15 years for a drug to go from the lab to regulatory approval. And more than 90% of drugs that enter clinical development fail. Just look at the headlines: one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies recently suffered three drug trial failures in a single week despite an enormous R&D budget, many talented scientists and a deep pipeline.

But this problem is far from unique to healthcare. In consumer tech, many startups flame out after a single hit; in automotive, EV pioneers are routinely outpaced by fast followers; digital investments in retail often fail to translate into customer growth.

The instinctive response when innovation fails is to do more of it: fund more projects, pursue more ideas, make more acquisitions and place more bets. If innovation is inherently unpredictable, the thinking goes, the best way to improve your chances of success is to increase the number of shots you take.

This kind of thinking is completely backward. It’s not about the shots. It’s about the target.

Imagine entering a darts tournament and throwing five consecutive bull’s-eyes, only to discover that you have been…
items.t: Vertex’s executive chairman: Here’s how we got our drug-trial success rate over 70% when the industry’s is 10% to 20%

items.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause

Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con?

‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live, billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee.

The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. (Fungi are big news in the menopause wellness world, often touted as an answer to brain fog. Though at best the scientific jury is still out, Ocado searches for lion’s mane mushrooms more than…
items.t: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause

items.title: She was a go-to Manhattan babysitter as a teen. Now she’s running a $100 million-a-year AI startup whose clients include the billionaire Koch family
items.summary:
From a nationwide FAA ground stop to Microsoft and Chase outages that disrupted millions of customers, a string of recent technology failures has highlighted the need to modernize aging infrastructure while raising new fears about the risks of an increasingly AI-dependent world.

But for Jaclyn Rice Nelson, cofounder and CEO of Tribe AI, that tension is exactly why businesses should embrace the technology—not run from it.

“I don’t think that anxiety around AI is unwarranted. I think it’s very real,” Nelson told Fortune .

“[AI] is ours to shape,” Nelson said. “And the only way you can shape it is if you understand it, and the only way you understand it is if you use it—and use it a lot.”

Nelson, 41, has built her business around helping companies do just that. Founded in 2019, Tribe AI has grown to a $100 million annual run rate by helping organizations—from Fortune 500s like Hyatt and MetLife to multibillion-dollar private conglomerates like Koch Inc.—put AI to work.

Tribe said on Nov. 18 that its annualized revenue had crossed $100 million, up 3.8 times from a year earlier, as more clients moved AI projects out of the pilot stage. “The hard part is getting AI into production inside a complex business,” Nelson said in the announcement.

Before building an AI startup, Nelson learned the value of hard work as a babysitter—and later at Google 

Nelson’s instinct to build something of her own predates the AI boom by decades.

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…
items.t: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage
items.t: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial

items.title: Alibaba and Tencent put their faith in Chinese chips as U.S. curbs threatens to slow down their AI development
items.summary:
Tencent and Alibaba said this week that domestic chips can cushion their cloud businesses from new U.S. restrictions on access to advanced AI processors, yet acknowledged that they could still slow the development of new AI models. 

Both tech giants reported earnings after the U.S. Department of Commerce released an interim rule expanding export controls on Monday, making them some of the first Chinese corporate responses to the restrictions. 

Chipmakers and exporters now need a license to sell advanced chips to data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The rule also requires a license for large data centers to offer substantial computing power to Chinese customers. Together, the measures are likely to restrict the amount of computing power available to Chinese companies like Alibaba and Tencent as they develop AI models and offer them to users.

Tencent 

Tencent executives, in the company’s earnings call, drew a distinction between the computing power needed to train new models and running existing ones.

“We actually don’t see an impact because our cloud business today is primarily running inference,” James Mitchell, Tencent’s chief strategy officer, told analysts on Wednesday. (Inference is the running of AI models, as opposed to training them.)

Mitchell added that Tencent had reached a stage where the inference could run on what he called a “surprisingly limited number” of domestically produced chips.

items.t: Alibaba and Tencent put their faith in Chinese chips as U.S. curbs threatens to slow down their AI development

items.title: Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy
items.summary:
Good morning. Intuit is unwinding its biggest acquisition while betting AI can help it win customers without owning the marketing platform it once viewed as central to that effort.

The QuickBooks and TurboTax parent announced Thursday it plans to sell Mailchimp, an email marketing automation platform, to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, subject to approval, with proceeds earmarked for fiscal 2027 share repurchases. Intuit paid approximately $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021. Mailchimp’s quarterly revenue fell 1% to $313 million.

Sasan Goodarzi, CEO of Intuit ( No. 231 on the Fortune 500) said on the earnings call that Intuit still wants to help businesses manage lead-to-cash needs, but believes it can do so more effectively by building AI-powered capabilities into QuickBooks rather than owning Mailchimp.

Mailchimp sale marks strategic shift 

The divestiture adds another dimension to what CFO Sandeep Aujla has called Intuit’s “reset to reaccelerate” strategy launched in August: accepting some near-term pressure on revenue per customer to rebuild customer acquisition. The strategy includes lower upfront revenue per TurboTax customer as Intuit seeks faster customer growth.

The latest results offered evidence of operating momentum. For the fiscal first quarter ended Oct. 31, revenue rose 12% to $4.35 billion, while adjusted earnings per share increased 56% to $2.91. Both exceeded analyst expectations.

In my conversation with Aujla, he pointed to mid-market revenue growth of 41% and customer growth of 30% as…
items.t: Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy
